newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Traffic jams, security and hugs open APEC.
newsitem.headline: Traffic jams, security and hugs open APEC.

text.p: Traffic snarls that left Filipino drivers choking in fury, strict security and invocations to the universal spirit of love on Wednesday heralded the fourth APEC summit.

"If APEC is here it is because it was meant to happen," said Corazon Juliano Soliman, leading an opening ritual at one of many conferences being held in conjunction with the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in the Philippine capital.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, China's Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and other leaders of APEC's 18 members will gather in Manila on Sunday before their annual summit at the Subic Bay special economic zone to the north on Monday.
The leaders will also hold one-on-one sessions, or bilaterals, including one between Clinton and Jiang.

On Wednesday, senior APEC officials met in the Philippine International Convention Centre in Manila to put finishing touches to a programme designed to produce concrete results to APEC's stated goal of lowering all trade barriers in the region by 2020.
APEC's foreign and trade ministers will meet in the convention centre on November 22-23 to put their imprimateur on an action plan the leaders are supposed to endorse at Subic.
The meeting is also expected to endorse a U.S. proposed common stance on information technology to be presented to the World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore next month.

Clinton, visiting Australia on his way to the Philippines, urged fellow Asia-Pacific leaders on Wednesday to spearhead their free trade push with cuts to barriers in the one trillion dollars a year information technology industry.
He told reporters after an hour-long meeting with Australian Prime Minister John Howard that APEC leaders must make progress towards their aim of axing trade barriers by 2020.
Hundreds of thousands of Manila residents were left wishing the annual bash aimed at helping to create the world's biggest free trade zone was not happening at all.
The normally impossible traffic in the Philippines was made even worse by the setting up of so-called "friendship lanes" where vehicles not bearing special APEC passes were banished.
"They may want to free trade but they don't have to do that by choking people in their cars. Because of these APEC lanes, I was stuck in traffic for three hours," one irate driver said.

The Philippines, which sees APEC as a coming out party for its own economic revival, has imposed strict security to prevent what officials say are plans by leftist groups to disrupt the event and embarrass the government of President Fidel Ramos.
Security officials accuse the left of trying to foment labour unrest and other protests.
Security was tight around the convention centre by the scenic Manila Bay, part of a complex of buildings erected during the authoritarian rule of the late President Ferdinand Marcos.

A personal project of then first lady Imelda Marcos, now a congresswoman but facing a jail term for corruption, the complex also includes a deserted former film centre many Filipinos believe is haunted.
Spirits of another sort were invoked at the opening of Code-NGO, the main parallel summit being organised by anti-APEC groups.
The group, which says representatives of some 5,000 regional non-government organisations will attend its conference, argues free trade is not a panacea and the poor need extra protection.

Their session, attended by only 75 people, began with a non-denominational prayer for enlightenment meant to "call on the Spirit Guide to walk and talk with us to confront the challenges of liberalisation", said Soliman, a veteran community organiser.
Delegates then sprinkled flower petals on each other and hugged.

APEC's 18 members are Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Mew Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
